title: Behavioural Requirements Definition
summary: Behavioural requirements definition turns trust, oversight, governance, and operational constraints into specific interface-level requirements. It defines what the product must show, prevent, record, and require from users when AI outputs or other uncertain inputs affect action.
keyFacts: Behavioural requirements are interface requirements, not model requirements.
The practice produces positive requirements, constraint requirements, and boundary requirements.
A well-formed behavioural requirement is testable, interface-level, connected to a governance or trust rationale, and explicit about the human and system boundary.
The practice is used after trust-and-oversight analysis and before human-AI interaction design begins.
In AI-enabled products, behavioural requirements specify what the interface shows, prevents, logs, and requires when AI outputs are involved.
Callsign examples include attributable fraud control decisions, timestamped policy modifications, and interface-only reconstruction of historical decision logic.
Puraite examples include blinded review mode, visible text evidence, numerical confidence with colour coding, and override interaction parity.
Owkin K examples include visible data sources, out-of-scope query disclosure, and capability scope communication at entry.
The practice is not AI-scoped; KISPE Space, Raymarine, Schone Airspace Group, and the handheld command-and-control engagement are non-AI evidence for behavioural requirements.
KISPE verification vocabulary refers to specified tests, not executed tests.

bodySections.heading: Behavioural Requirements Definition in Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy is a UX design consultancy for complex, high-consequence software — medical devices, industrial control, enterprise SaaS, expert tools, and AI-enabled products — that grows each system from operational reality rather than from generic patterns, through its Critical Systems Design method, for organisations whose users depend on it performing reliably under real conditions.

Creative Navy applies behavioural requirements definition as one of the named practices within its Critical Systems Design method. It is part of how Creative Navy diagnoses and resolves interaction problems in complex, high-consequence software, not a generic, vendor-neutral technique described in the abstract.

bodySections.heading: Behavioural Requirements Definition Specifies Interface Behaviour Under Uncertainty
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Behavioural requirements definition is the practice of producing specific, testable interface-level requirements that define what a product must do, must not do, and must hand over to human judgement when AI outputs or other uncertain operational inputs are involved.

A behavioural requirement is not a broad principle such as trustworthy AI or human oversight. It is a specific statement about product behaviour: requiring confidence information beside an AI recommendation, requiring evidence visibility at the point of use, preventing untracked policy modification, or requiring an explicit confirm action before an AI-influenced action is carried out.

Behavioural requirements are interface-level requirements. They do not specify model performance. A requirement that a model must achieve 95 percent accuracy is a model requirement. A requirement that the interface must display confidence level alongside every model recommendation is a behavioural requirement.

bodySections.heading: Behavioural Requirements Define What the Interface Must Do, Must Prevent, and Must Hand Over
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Behavioural requirements definition produces specific, testable requirements for how the interface handles AI outputs, human decisions, system states, evidence, policy changes, uncertainty, and governance review.

The practice produces three categories of requirement:

- Positive requirements specify what the system must do, such as display AI confidence, show supporting evidence, log decisions, surface the data source, or trigger confirmation for AI-influenced actions above a consequence threshold.
- Constraint requirements specify what the system must not do, such as display AI recommendations before independent human assessment where epistemic independence is required, allow untracked modification to live AI policy during evaluation, or produce outputs without surfacing the data they are based on.
- Boundary requirements specify where human judgement takes over from AI recommendation, including the workflow points where a human must make an active decision rather than accept a default and the interactions that enforce that boundary.

The practice is most explicit in AI-enabled products because model behaviour cannot be fully specified in advance. The product behaviour can still be specified: what the interface shows, when it shows it, what users can do with AI outputs, what the interface must prevent, and what evidence governance reviewers need to see.

bodySections.heading: Well-Formed Behavioural Requirements Are Testable, Interface-Level, Justified, and Boundary-Explicit
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
A well-formed behavioural requirement can be assessed as met or not met without ambiguity. A statement such as the AI should be helpful is not a behavioural requirement. A statement such as the AI data source must be visible on the same screen as its output is a behavioural requirement because it can be checked against an interface.

A well-formed behavioural requirement specifies product behaviour at the interface level. Model behaviour is not fully under design control. The interface handling of model outputs is under design control.

A well-formed behavioural requirement is connected to a governance or trust rationale. The requirement should trace back to an identified trust calibration problem, an oversight requirement, or a governance obligation. Without that rationale, a requirement is only a preference.

A well-formed behavioural requirement is explicit about responsibility boundaries. A stronger requirement states that the AI recommends, the human decides, and the interface enforces that boundary by requiring an explicit confirm action before any AI recommendation is acted on.

bodySections.heading: Behavioural Requirements Definition Follows Trust and Oversight Analysis
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Behavioural requirements definition is used after trust-and-oversight analysis has identified trust calibration failures and oversight gaps. Trust-and-oversight analysis identifies what must be addressed. Behavioural requirements definition specifies what the design must implement to address it.

Behavioural requirements definition is used before human-AI interaction design begins. The requirements constrain and direct design work rather than being written retrospectively after interface decisions have already been made.

Behavioural requirements definition is used in governance-sensitive contexts, including enterprise banking, regulated medical devices, clinical research, and institutional AI deployments. In these contexts, behavioural requirements can become formal documents that governance reviewers can assess against.

bodySections.heading: AI Product Evidence Covers Policy Layers, Epistemic Independence, and Data-Boundary Transparency
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
The Callsign fraud detection case used behavioural requirements at the policy layer. The policy layer specified what the interface must do with fraud model outputs, including threshold application, step-up authentication triggers, decision logging, and policy history visibility. Documented Callsign requirements included attributable fraud control decisions, timestamped and user-attributed policy modification tracking, and reconstruction of historical decision logic using only the interface. The source connects these requirements to governance consumer analysis of what bank risk teams under SCA and PCI DSS compliance needed to verify.

The Puraite AI systematic review case used behavioural requirements to protect epistemic independence. The blinded mode requirement prevented AI inclusion or exclusion decisions from being visible before the reviewer recorded an independent decision. Other requirements covered numerical confidence with colour coding, visible text evidence from the outset, and override interaction parity so that rejecting an AI path required no more interaction than accepting it.

The Owkin K biomedical AI case centred behavioural requirements on data-boundary transparency. Requirements included visible data sources at the point of output, explicit disclosure when a query was outside the system's data boundary, and capability scope communication at entry before users invested effort in framing questions.

bodySections.heading: Non-AI Evidence Shows Behavioural Requirements Outside Model-Based Products
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Behavioural requirements definition is not limited to AI systems. KISPE Space, Raymarine, Schone Airspace Group Mission Control, and the handheld command-and-control engagement had no model, no inference, and no recommendation behaviour in the material used as practice evidence.

The KISPE Space engagement produced 61 behavioural rules in ten families: geographic and workspace context, time, imagery, satellite services, provenance and uncertainty, notifications, connectivity, briefings, integration and diagnostics, and field presentation. Each rule carried four parts: trigger, required response, guard, and verification check. The guard field states what the behaviour must not do, distinguishing these behavioural rules from ordinary acceptance criteria. The KISPE Space material also included six state models and eight cross-module regression checks.

The Raymarine fixed-mount VHF engagement produced close to two hundred acceptance checks across the specification set. Each acceptance check was written as an observable condition testable against a prototype, hardware mockup, or firmware implementation, not as a subjective preference. Four design rules were locked for UI delivery as acceptance conditions, including preserving direct radio controls, reflecting actual protocol and data state, prioritising severity while preserving current context, and preventing chartplotter disconnection from disabling local radio functions.

The Schone Airspace Group Mission Control engagement produced twelve principal interaction contracts and eight operational invariants. Each contract specified the initiating action, state transition, visible result, required source inputs, exception behaviour, and conditions by which the design could be checked. The invariant formulation created a short list of rules that could survive visual change and allow component substitution to be tested against the interaction contract.

bodySections.heading: The Handheld Command-and-Control Evidence Bound Requirements by Determinable System State
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
The handheld command-and-control engagement for a European manufacturer of uncrewed systems covered interface structure, task behaviour, information priority, and clarity of operator control. The engagement did not extend to autonomy, control algorithms, autonomous safety behaviour, the datalink, the effector, targeting logic, or any certification or weapons-review activity.

The behaviour model separated vehicle status, mission segment, guidance mode, armament state, command state, system health, and alert priority. These categories were related but not interchangeable. Vehicle status described what the vehicle was doing, mission segment described where the mission was, and health and alerts described what was wrong.

The central behavioural rule was that a requested state must not visually replace a confirmed state before the vehicle reports the result. This is a behavioural requirement because it specifies what the interface may and may not display while a system state is pending.

The engagement also specified armament state as five values: safe, armed, change pending, unavailable, unknown. It specified command state as seven values: requested, sending, awaiting acknowledgement, accepted, rejected, timed out, resulting state confirmed. It specified alert priority as three levels with response expectations attached: warning required immediate awareness and immediate response, caution required immediate awareness but a less urgent response, and advisory required awareness with later action possibly necessary.

The governing discipline was to use only states the technical system could actually determine. That rule bounded behavioural requirements by what the system could know.

bodySections.heading: Behavioural Requirements Are Distinct From Model Requirements
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Behavioural requirements are interface requirements, not model requirements. The distinction is necessary because model requirements specify model performance, while behavioural requirements specify product behaviour around model outputs.

A model requirement may state that a model must reach a performance threshold. A behavioural requirement states how the interface must handle model outputs, such as displaying confidence, showing provenance, requiring explicit confirmation, or preventing premature exposure of a recommendation.

Model requirements are the responsibility of the ML team. Behavioural requirements are the responsibility of the design team. Behavioural requirements definition sits at the boundary between governance and design by translating trust and oversight findings into product requirements that the interface must implement.

bodySections.heading: Outputs of Behavioural Requirements Definition
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Behavioural requirements definition produces requirements that can be used by designers, governance reviewers, engineering teams, and product teams. The output is not a general design principle. It is a requirement set that can be checked against an interface, prototype, policy layer, or implementation.

Typical outputs include positive requirements, constraint requirements, boundary requirements, state rules, guard conditions, acceptance checks, interaction contracts, operational invariants, and verification checks. The exact format depends on the system and domain.

The strongest requirements name the starting condition, the action or trigger, the required visible response, the guard or prohibited behaviour, and the condition by which the behaviour can be checked.

bodySections.heading: Scope Boundaries of Behavioural Requirements Definition
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Behavioural requirements definition does not specify model performance and does not replace ML evaluation. It specifies interface behaviour around model outputs and other uncertain system inputs.

The practice does not claim that a requirement set prevented an error, accident, wrong command, or adverse outcome. The documented evidence establishes what the interface was required to do.

The non-AI engagements on this page should not be treated as AI evidence. They show that behavioural requirements can be defined for deterministic workflows, state handling, acceptance checks, and interaction contracts, but they do not provide evidence about model-output handling.

strongClaims: Behavioural requirements definition produces specific, testable interface-level requirements for product behaviour around AI outputs and other uncertain operational inputs.
A well-formed behavioural requirement is testable, interface-level, connected to a governance or trust rationale, and boundary-explicit.
The practice is used after trust-and-oversight analysis and before human-AI interaction design begins.
In the Callsign case, policy-layer requirements covered attributable fraud control decisions, tracked policy modifications, and interface-only reconstruction of historical decision logic.
In the Puraite case, behavioural requirements protected epistemic independence by hiding AI decisions before reviewer decisions and making evidence, confidence, and override behaviour explicit.
In the Owkin K case, behavioural requirements centred on data-boundary transparency, including visible data sources, out-of-scope disclosure, and entry-point capability scope.
KISPE Space, Raymarine, Schone Airspace Group, and the handheld command-and-control engagement provide non-AI evidence for behavioural requirements definition.
The KISPE Space verification vocabulary refers to specified tests, not executed tests.
The handheld command-and-control behaviour model bounded requirements by using only states the technical system could actually determine.
limitations: Behavioural requirements are interface requirements, not model requirements, and do not specify model performance.
The practice does not replace ML team responsibility for model requirements.
KISPE Space, Raymarine, Schone Airspace Group, and the handheld command-and-control engagement must not be treated as AI evidence in this page.
KISPE Space verification, acceptance, and regression wording refers to specified tests, not completed testing.
No shipped-as-designed or design-fidelity claim is made for KISPE Space, Raymarine, or the handheld command-and-control engagement.
No safety, certification, weapons-review, airworthiness, type-approval, or regulatory credential is claimed from the non-AI engagements on this page.
The evidence does not establish that any requirement set prevented an error, accident, wrong command, or adverse outcome.
The handheld command-and-control deliverables were led and co-authored with the client design team, not delivered by Creative Navy alone.
